newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: ICRC urges Afghan factions to respect rights.
newsitem.headline: ICRC urges Afghan factions to respect rights.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross urged warring Afghan factions on Wednesday to respect basic humanitarian principles and international law.

Michel Ducraux, head of the ICRC delegation in Kabul, told a news conference he was deeply concerned at recent air raids on residential areas of Kabul and the northeastern city of Taloqan and at the refusal of factions to let the ICRC visit prisoners.
"The ICRC firmly believes that diving into barbarity will not by any means help the people of Afghanistan to find a way out of the present tragedy," he said.

Ducraux said the ICRC had been unable to visit about 1,000 prisoners held by warring parties for the past two months, despite negotiations with the ruling Islamic Taleban militia and the northern opposition alliance.
However, he said ICRC delegates had been allowed to tend about 200 wounded prisoners held in the north by anti-Taleban forces and also to see wounded prisoners in Taleban hands.
Ducraux said it was vital for fighters to be given precise orders to avert the risk of abuses, including summary executions, by men acting under the stress of combat.
He appealed to all sides to observe a minimum respect for civilians, wounded people and prisoners and not to consider their captives as a bargaining chip in negotiations.
"They have to stick to their responsibilities unilaterally and spontaneously without asking for reciprocity," he said.
Efforts to arrange peace talks between the Taleban and their opponents have foundered on the Islamic militia's insistence that opposition forces must first agree to a prisoner exchange.

Taleban leaders say they are particularly anxious to secure the release of several colleagues, including foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous, captured when opposition forces drove the Taleban from the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif in May.
The purist Islamic Taleban captured Kabul last September and now control more than two thirds of the country.
